summary:
Article 11 of Ecuador's 2008 Constitution binds the state to respect differences of ethnicity, nationality, social and generational standing and gender, expressly including sexual orientation and gender identity. The provision sits in a secular, multinational constitutional order and is the foundation on which LGBTI claims are litigated. Same-sex sexual activity was decriminalised in 1997, when Constitutional Tribunal Case No. 111-97-TC struck Article 516 of the Penal Code, and the 1998 Constitution made Ecuador the first country in the Americas to bar discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation.

Legal gender recognition has operated on self-determination since the 2016 Gender Identity Law, which permits a change of legal gender and birth name on identity documents without surgery or medical diagnosis. The National Assembly's reforms of 12 December 2023 to the Organic Law on Identity Management and Civil Data, regulated by a decree President Daniel Noboa issued on 11 June 2024, streamlined the civil-registry procedure that carries out the change. That procedure is the operative route for a trans visitor or resident updating Ecuadorian records.

Access for adolescents is in motion. Constitutional Court rulings reported by AP in April 2026 allowed trans adolescents to change name and sex on official records, in a case described as opening a path for others seeking recognition. Outright International's country overview, updated 12 March 2026, still records legal gender recognition as unavailable to under-18s. The sources do not establish how far the rulings extend beyond the case decided.

Partner recognition is split. Same-sex marriage has been legal since 2019, but adoption is constitutionally restricted to different-sex couples under Article 68, and legislation passed on 14 August 2026 by 118 votes to 0 explicitly bars single people and same-sex couples from adopting. That statute sits against a 2018 Constitutional Court decision, taken 5-3 with one abstention, ordering the Civil Registry to register a girl as the daughter of a lesbian couple; in May 2018 the court ordered registration of Satya Amani Bicknell Rothon, the daughter of Helen Bicknell and Nicola Rothon, with the couple's lawyer arguing that refusal violated the child's rights. A trans visitor in what would locally be classed as a same-sex relationship can expect the marriage to be recognised and parentage through adoption to be closed.

Conversion practices are criminalised. Article 151 of the Penal Code, in force since 2014, treats them as equivalent to torture and carries 7 to 10 years' imprisonment. Enforcement is weak: as of 2023 hundreds of clinics still promoted the practice, and clinics have confined young people against their will, including a case in which parents unsuccessfully sought their daughter's release.

Violence against LGBTQ Ecuadorians was reported to be increasing in January 2024 amid the country's internal armed conflict. The US State Department's 2011 human rights report recorded discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation among Ecuador's societal problems, and LGBT groups at that time said police and prosecutors did not thoroughly investigate deaths of LGBT individuals. No source in this inventory supplies a trans-specific violence count with a denominator that would allow comparison against the general homicide rate.

Detention carries specific risk. Trans women are held in an almost universally male prison system, in male spaces and pavilions, and report gender-identity discrimination, unsafe placement, sexual violence, forced suppression of gender expression and barriers to health care. The July 2016 government decision to develop protocols for LGBT people deprived of liberty has not produced consistent practice; the trans-rights organisation Silueta X, through its PrisioTrans programme, advocates individualised housing decisions applying Inter-American standards and weighing gender identity, safety, the detainee's own assessment and informed consent, rather than a single placement rule.
tangentialFactors:
The gap between the 2019 marriage ruling and the adoption prohibition is the sharpest fault line in Ecuadorian LGBTI law: a relationship is recognised for some purposes and excluded from parental status for others, and the 2026 statute passed without a dissenting vote.

Conversion-practice enforcement is the clearest case of a criminal prohibition without operational effect. A penalty of 7 to 10 years has coexisted since 2014 with hundreds of clinics advertising the practice in 2023.

The internal armed conflict that began in early 2024 changed the security environment in which anti-LGBTQ violence occurs; the reporting links the rise in violence to that conflict rather than to any change in the legal regime.

Official treatment of public assembly runs the other way. Pride marches have been authorised in all major cities with police protection and official participation, and in 2013 presidential candidate Nelson Zavala was fined more than $3,000 and barred from office for a year for calling gay people "sinners" and "immoral".
localsOnly:
Ecuador's last prison census counted 73 trans women across the entire prison system, a figure the organisation Fundación Vivir Libre says substantially understates the population; trans women are placed in male pavilions.

Named cases document the pattern. Trans woman Helen Maldonado died during the November 2021 massacre at Penitenciaría del Litoral while held in a male prison space. A 2022 complaint concerned cruel, inhuman and degrading treatment of trans women at Lago Agrio. Allegations in 2024 described forced head-shaving, beatings and violence targeting breast and body implants. A 23-year-old trans woman died in state custody in 2026 at the El Encuentro maximum-security prison, prompting calls for an independent investigation.

A Venezuelan trans woman, 27, detained in August 2023 at Penitenciaría del Litoral was initially placed in male pavilion 9 with three other trans women rather than the "prioritaria" pavilion reserved for vulnerable populations, where many sexo-gender-diverse inmates are held; she received no medical examination and no HIV treatment there. Rapes and torture reported in the investigation were directed at prisoners' gender identity, and protective placement was applied unevenly.

Residents also face the adoption bar, the conversion-clinic sector, and an education system in which the State Department found LGBT people's equal access frequently violated in 2011. The age of consent is 14 regardless of gender or sexual orientation.

Trans political participation has a track record: Diane Marie Rodríguez Zambrano became the first openly transgender candidate in 2013 and the first transgender lawmaker in 2017.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory documents airport or border screening practice, document-marker flagging or body-search procedure as it affects trans travellers to Ecuador; that remains unsourced.

The scope of the 2026 Constitutional Court rulings on adolescents is unresolved: AP describes a path-opening decision while Outright's March 2026 overview continues to state that legal gender recognition is unavailable to under-18s.

Trans-specific violence data for Ecuador is not available in a form that supports comparison with the general homicide rate; the January 2024 reporting establishes a direction of travel, not a magnitude.

The 2011 State Department report is the most recent official assessment in this inventory and predates the 2016 gender identity law, the 2019 marriage ruling and the 2024 security emergency.
